sentences.text: The ermine came down the scree in November and went up again in March and in between she was somewhere on the mountain with her mouth full.
Everybody in the valley had seen her at least once.
She was not shy and she was not hiding; she went along the top of the dry-stone walls in broad daylight with the confidence of something that has never been caught.
In summer she was brown with a white front.

From the first snow she was white all over except the tip of the tail, which stayed black, and which was the only part of her you could actually see against a drift — a small black comma travelling along a wall at speed with nothing attached to it.
And from November she carried the thaw.
You could see it if she stopped, which she did about once a minute, sitting up on her back legs the way they do to look at you.
There was something in her jaws.

It was not large — the size of a hen's egg, perhaps — and it was not any colour, which is the difficulty; Lise had looked at it four times at close range over three winters and could only ever say that it was the same colour as the day after tomorrow.
It was warm.
You could tell from a distance of two metres.

On the coldest morning of the year, standing at the wall with the frost cracking in the grass, you could feel it on your face like an open oven door, coming off a thing the size of an egg being carried by an animal that weighed less than a cup of coffee.

Lise had tried, once, at nine, to work out how she could carry something that warm in her mouth all winter without it doing her any harm, and had been told by her father to stop asking questions of that kind about that particular animal.
She had not stopped.
She had simply stopped asking him.
She would not put it down.
That was the whole of the arrangement and everybody in the valley knew it.

She would carry it all winter, up and down the scree, through the snow and under it, without ever setting it down for a second — not to eat, not to sleep, not for anything — until somebody came up and asked her, properly, to let it go.
And then it would be spring.
Not in a week.
Not gradually.

There were photographs in the parish office, four of them, taken by a man called Anton in the 1960s who had been a serious person about photography: the same view of the same slope on four consecutive days, and on the third one there is snow to the wall-top and on the fourth one there is grass, and everybody who sees them for the first time says the same thing, which is that the man had obviously cheated.
He had not cheated.

The four negatives are in the same strip, in order, with the frame numbers on them, and they have been looked at by two people from a university who came up in 2003 and were extremely polite and went away again.
What happens is not that the snow melts.

Melting takes days and leaves the ground wet and the drifts hollowed out and grey at the edges, and everybody in that valley has watched melting happen every spring of their lives and knows exactly what it looks like.
The snow goes.
There is no water.
That is the part that nobody from outside believes and that nobody inside bothers arguing about.
The ground under it is dry.
